name: Azelaic acid scalp

lead: Azelaic acid is a skin treatment for acne, rosacea and hyperpigmentation. Hair-loss forum users apply it to the scalp or add it to stacks, hoping for a mild finasteride-like effect that slows thinning.

The claim comes from a 1988 lab study in which azelaic acid combined with zinc sulfate strongly inhibited 5-alpha-reductase in human skin. No pattern-hair-loss trials were found; a small early trial in central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia, a scarring alopecia, is registered.

paras: It is applied topically to the scalp, usually as an add-on to other hair-loss products, the same way it is used on skin for acne or rosacea. Users treat it as a long-term routine step.
Dryness and irritation are the main reported effects.

angle.text: Hair-loss forum users add azelaic acid to scalp stacks, believing it mildly blocks 5-alpha-reductase like finasteride does, to slow thinning and reduce DHT at the scalp. The enzyme claim comes from lab work. It is studied for acne and rosacea, and no scalp trials test it for pattern hair loss.

lead: Azelaic acid is a dicarboxylic acid used topically at 15 to 20 percent for acne, rosacea and hyperpigmentation.[1] In hair-loss communities it is applied to the scalp or included in compounded anti-hair-loss lotions with the aim of slowing thinning and keeping hair density, because of claims that it mildly inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme targeted by finasteride and dutasteride.[2][3]

Wikipedia cites a 1988 in vitro report in which azelaic acid combined with zinc sulfate strongly inhibited 5-alpha-reductase in human skin; the article notes this is a single in vitro study and not clinical evidence that topical azelaic acid alone has this effect in vivo.[1] A forum poster in 2000 asked about a French study combining zinc, vitamin B6 and azelaic acid reported to lower scalp DHT, showing how the idea circulated early.[4]

A small early phase 1 trial of azelaic acid in central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA), a scarring alopecia, is registered.[5] Lifting forums mention azelaic acid in compounded topical mixes with minoxidil, tretinoin and finasteride, usually discussed by people also dealing with hair thinning from anabolic use.[2][6]
infobox: Wheat, rye, barley; produced by Malassezia furfur[1]

paras: Topical azelaic acid treats mild to moderate acne, papulopustular rosacea, melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.[1]

Users discuss scalp application as a mild anti-androgen add-on. One T Nation poster suggests having a compounding pharmacy mix 10% minoxidil, tretinoin, azelaic acid, 0.1% finasteride, biotin and hydrocortisone into a single lotion, and another asks whether topical azelaic acid cream can control scalp DHT and whether it is safe for someone on testosterone therapy.[2][3] No approved hair-loss indication exists for azelaic acid.

Reported actions include bacteriostatic activity, normalising follicular keratinisation, reducing reactive oxygen species and cytokines, and tyrosinase inhibition.[1] The 5-alpha-reductase claim rests on the 1988 in vitro combination study.[1]
Skin dryness and irritation are the main reported effects, particularly in people with eczema.[1]

sections.h: Use in hair-loss and lifting communities
paras: On T Nation, azelaic acid comes up in threads about hair loss during testosterone therapy or anabolic cycles, where members list it among options beyond the 'big 3' of finasteride, minoxidil and ketoconazole shampoo, and a 2016 T Nation article on hair loss summarises treatments.[6][7] Members also share a recalled report of a zinc, B6 and azelaic acid combination.[4] These are personal and secondhand accounts.

A registered early phase 1 trial (NCT05416333) is testing azelaic acid in CCCA in 18 participants; it began in 2024 and is listed as active, not recruiting, and no results were loaded for this article.[5] No studies found of azelaic acid for androgenetic alopecia in the sources used.

lore.intro: Azelaic acid appears in T Nation hair-loss threads and compounded-topical suggestions as a mild 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor.[2][3][4]

claims.claim: Azelaic acid on the scalp acts as a mild 5-ARI and lowers scalp DHT.
Azelaic acid can be combined with minoxidil, tretinoin and finasteride in a compounded lotion.

timeline.event: In vitro report of azelaic acid plus zinc sulfate inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase.[1]
